newsitem.title: USA: Dole speaks to Ohio newspaper editors.
newsitem.headline: Dole speaks to Ohio newspaper editors.

text.p: Republican candidate Bob Dole, in an interview published on Wednesday, said President Bill Clinton's foreign policy was in disarray and the United States was losing credibility.

"Northern Ireland -- we don't have a ceasefire. Things have gone to pot in North Korea. They have nuclear reactors. Cuba. I mean I can't point to the foreign policy success in this administration," he said.

"It seems to me if we're going to have a foreign policy, we've got to follow up on it day by day," the challenger said. "It's got to be responsible. Otherwise we're losing credibility. We've lost a lot of credibility."

Dole made the comments in a meeting with the editorial board of The Plain Dealer on Tuesday after his latest Ohio campaign stop. The Cleveland newspaper on Wednesday published a partial transcript of the interview.
Dole also said Clinton had not achieved U.S. goals in Somalia, Haiti, Bosnia or Iraq.

On Iraq, Dole said, Saddam Hussein is stronger now than he was two months ago and nuclear inspection requirements have not been enforced. "We know they haven't had an inspection since June," Dole said.
"Mission creep" in Somalia changed a humanitarian mission to nation building, and billions sent to Haiti have not improved conditions there, he added.
"And the Bosnian conflict, for better or worse. Clinton said he was going to lift the arms embargo, let the people defend themselves. When he got elected he didn't do anything," Dole said.
"Are the right people going to be in power" after "so-called elections" in Bosnia, Dole asked, adding that he does not expect Bosnian elections to change the situation.

Asked what the overall strategic aims of American foreign policy should be, Dole said, "First of all, it's got to be in our interest. Obviously you can't kick every sleeping dog around the world. We can't be the world's police, let's put it that way."
But, he said, when there is a national interest, the United States must make a commitment and follow up on it.
On domestic issues, Dole told the newspaper he believes his proposal for federally funded school vouchers could withstand a constitutional challenge.
Dole wants to offer low- and low-middle-income parents help in paying tuition at the public, private or religious school of their choice.

Comparing the plan to the GI Bill that enabled veterans to attend college, Dole said, "It's not federal control of education, but it's an experiment, a demonstration project which we would do for five years. See if it works. My view is we'll meet the constitutional challenge."
